title: Is B tuned to A's station?
allegory: A composition score is like checking how much of one radio station a second radio actually picks up, with the volume knobs divided out, so only the tuning counts; and because random radios catch some static anyway, you always compare against them.
map: the few stations head A broadcasts on
the output subspace of A's W_OV, rank at most d_head
the stations head B's radio is tuned to
the subspace B reads: its W_QK for Q- or K-composition, its W_OV for V-composition
how much of A's broadcast B picks up, volume ignored
static that random radios pick up anyway
the random-matrix baseline every score must beat

cap.1: Two parts of a model sit in different layers. Does the later one actually listen to what the earlier one says? Can you tell just from the wiring?
cap.2: Heads never talk directly; they read and write a shared residual stream. Composition asks whether a later head reads the subspace an earlier head writes.
cap.3: A composition score answers from weights alone, with no data: do the earlier head's W_OV output directions align with the directions the later head's W_QK or W_OV reads?

cap.1: Head A broadcasts on a few stations. Head B's radio is tuned to a few stations. The question is how much of A's broadcast B actually picks up.
cap.2: A writes into a small subspace (rank at most d_head) of the residual stream; B reads through its own small subspace. Overlap between them is composition.
cap.3: W_OV^A has rank ≤ d_head, and so does B's input map. The score measures how A's column space aligns with B's row space, weighted by their singular values.

cap.1: Top: how much of A's signal comes out of B. Bottom: A's volume times B's sensitivity. Dividing means only the tuning counts, not the loudness.
cap.2: These are Frobenius norms: the square root of the sum of every entry squared. Dividing makes the score run from 0 to 1, blind to how big either matrix is.
cap.3: ‖AB‖_F ≤ ‖A‖_F ‖B‖_F, so the score lies in [0, 1]. W_A is the earlier head's W_OV; W_B is the later head's W_QK (Q- or K-composition) or W_OV (V-composition).

chapters.name: Static on the line
chapters.verdict: A composition score means nothing until you know what random scores.

cap.1: Even two radios tuned at random pick up some of each other's static. So a score only means something next to what random tuning gives.
cap.2: Random matrices of the same shape give clearly non-zero scores. [1.2] has you compute that baseline first, then look for pairs that stand well above it.
cap.3: In high but finite dimensions, random low-rank subspaces still overlap, so the score under random weights is clearly above 0. Compare against it before reading any heatmap.

cap.1: Score every pair of an early head and a late head, subtract the static, and one bright cell stands out: the previous-token head feeding the induction head.
cap.2: Head 1.4's keys read the subspace head 0.7 writes to: K-composition, the heart of the induction circuit, spotted from weights before any experiment.
cap.3: Activations agree: decomposing layer-1 attention scores by (query, key) component, the (Embed, L0H7) pair dominates, and W_Eᵀ W_QK^1.4 W_OV^0.7 W_E is checked with top_1_acc.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Then test the guess by patching

cap.1: Composition scores let you guess which parts talk to each other before running anything. Then you check the guess with experiments.
cap.2: A cheap, data-free map of who might feed whom, handy for choosing what to patch. Its lesson travels: every similarity score needs a random baseline.
cap.3: Weight-based composition generates circuit hypotheses you later ablate, patch or steer. The baseline habit carries over to probes, SAE features and any overlap measured in high dimensions.

coda.title: Set how well B is tuned to A, then widen the airwaves

params.label: tuning: overlap of A's write and B's read direction

caption.1: Set how well B is tuned to A, then change how wide the airwaves are. The dark curve is what random tuning scores. Only a score far above it means anything.
caption.2: Random directions overlap less as the stream widens, but never reach zero. A score of 0.3 is below random at width 4 and many times above it at width 500.
caption.3: Rank-1 toy: score = |cos| between write and read directions, and for random directions E|cos| ≈ √(2/πd). Real heads are rank-d_head maps, so compute the baseline empirically for your shapes.

where_else: K-composition between previous-token heads and induction heads
Q- and V-composition: the same score with the later head's queries or values
Comparing a probe direction or steering vector with an SAE feature by overlap
Any similarity in high dimensions, where random vectors are nearly but never exactly orthogonal

hamming.what: A number from 0 to 1 for how much of what one head writes lands where a later head reads, computed from weights alone.
hamming.when: When you want a data-free first guess at which heads compose, such as a previous-token head feeding an induction head.
hamming.why: It turns 'these heads might talk' into a checkable score, provided you compare it with what random matrices score.

object.title: The broadcast sheet
object.subtitle: Head A can only write on a flat sheet of directions; each reader catches as much as lies along it.

clusters.label: residual stream (3 of its many dimensions)

arrows.label: unrelated head: almost out of it

cap.1: Head A can only write on a flat sheet of directions, its output plane. Everything it says lands somewhere on that sheet.
cap.2: W_OV of head A has rank at most d_head, so its outputs span a small subspace of the residual stream.
cap.3: The column space of W_OV^A: a d_head-dimensional subspace of the d_model-dimensional stream, drawn as a plane in 3-D.

cap.1: Head 1.4 reads along a direction lying almost flat in A's sheet. It hears nearly everything A says: high composition.
cap.2: When B reads mostly from A's output subspace, ‖W_A W_B‖ stays close to ‖W_A‖·‖W_B‖: a score near the top.
cap.3: High score: B's row space is well aligned with A's column space along their large singular directions.

cap.1: An unrelated head reads almost straight up, out of the sheet. It barely hears A: a low score.
cap.2: Directions nearly orthogonal to A's subspace pass little of A's output, so ‖W_A W_B‖ is small.
cap.3: Low score: B's read directions are close to the orthogonal complement of A's column space.

cap.1: A reader pointed at random still catches some of the sheet. That leftover is the static every score has to beat.
cap.2: Random directions overlap any subspace a little, so random matrices give non-zero scores: the baseline.
cap.3: A random unit vector's squared overlap with a k-dim subspace of R^d averages k/d: small, never zero.

cap.1: Real airwaves are hundreds of dimensions wide, so the static is fainter, but it never vanishes.
cap.2: Wider streams lower the baseline, which is why you compute it for your model's actual shapes.
cap.3: Compare against scores from random matrices with the same shapes and scale, as [1.2] does, before reading any heatmap.

predict.q: Two random matrices of the right shapes get a composition score. What do you expect?
predict.why: Random subspaces still overlap a little in finite dimensions, so you need a random baseline before believing a score.

predict.q: B's read directions lie almost entirely inside A's output plane. The score is:
predict.why: Almost everything A writes lands where B reads, so ‖W_A W_B‖ is close to ‖W_A‖·‖W_B‖.

predict.q: You double every weight in head A. What happens to the composition score?

options.t: Nothing: the norms cancel it out

predict.why: The score divides by ‖W_A‖, so only the alignment counts, not the loudness.

object.where: Any 'does this output feed that input?' question in high dimensions: probes, steering vectors, SAE features.
